messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Crowding: Crowded places, Moral Violation: People misbehaving
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Koa was fifty-three years old, a captain for a major airline, and had been married to his wife, Leilani, for twenty-eight years. He came to therapy at her insistence, though he would not have said so himself. He had been a pilot for over thirty years, a career built on precision, control, and the absolute trust of hundreds of passengers at a time. That trust had been shattered in a way he could never have anticipated, and now the very things that made him good at his job—his vigilance, his attention to detail, his ability to remain calm under pressure—had turned against him.

The event that had undone him happened five years ago, during a layover in a country he had flown into dozens of times. He had been taken by men in uniforms, accused of something he did not understand, and held for three days. They had not asked for information. They had not demanded a confession. They had simply wanted to break him. He remembered the smell of diesel fuel and stale sweat, the way it clung to the concrete room where they kept him. He remembered the sound of boots on the floor, the rhythm of it, and the way silence would fall just before the door opened. He remembered the photographs they took of him—flash, then darkness, then another flash—and how those images had burned themselves into his mind so that now, when the memory returned, it was not like remembering at all. It was like looking at a photograph, perfectly clear, perfectly still, and perfectly unbearable. The emotion that came with it was so overwhelming that he had learned to stop whatever he was doing, to freeze, to wait for it to pass, because if he did not, he was afraid he would fall apart entirely.

In the months that followed, Koa had returned to flying. He had no choice. It was his career, his identity, his livelihood. But the cockpit, once a sanctuary of order and routine, had become a place of constant threat monitoring. He found himself watching his first officer too closely, scanning the cabin crew for any sign of unusual behavior, reading the faces of passengers as they boarded as though he could detect a weapon or a plan. He knew it was irrational. He knew the people around him were not the men who had taken him. But the feeling would not go away. He had come to believe that danger lived in the ordinary—in the sudden quiet of the cabin during a long-haul flight, in the way a passenger might hesitate before taking their seat, in the silence of a hotel room after a long day of flying. Silence, for Koa, had become a signal. It meant something was about to happen. It meant the door would open.

At home, the symptoms had taken a different shape. He checked the locks on every door and window before bed, sometimes three or four times, and then again when he woke in the middle of the night. Leilani had learned not to mention it. She had learned not to cry in front of him, because the sight of her tears—anyone’s tears—sent a spike of alarm through him that he could not explain. Crying felt like a prelude to something worse, a signal that control had been lost. He avoided crowded places entirely. Grocery stores, airports during peak hours, even family gatherings had become unmanageable. He had stopped attending his daughter’s college events because the auditorium was too full, and the noise and proximity of so many bodies made him feel like he was back in that room. He had also developed a sharp intolerance for what he called “people misbehaving”—any violation of social order, any argument in public, any raised voice or rude gesture. It did not matter how minor. It felt like a crack in the fabric of safety, and he could not tolerate it.

The consequences had accumulated slowly. He had been passed over for a promotion to chief pilot because he had declined the required training program—it involved several weeks of classroom instruction in a crowded building, and he could not bring himself to say yes. He told himself it was not worth the stress. Leilani had stopped inviting him to social events. Their conversations had grown shorter, more careful. She had told him, the week before he came to see me, that she felt like she was living with a stranger who was always waiting for something terrible to happen.

What finally brought Koa to seek help was not the avoidance or the hypervigilance or the lost promotion. It was a moment in the cockpit, at 35,000 feet, when the cabin went quiet during a night flight and he felt his heart stop. He had gripped the yoke so hard his hands ached, certain that something was about to break through the door. Nothing happened. The flight landed safely. But he knew, for the first time, that he could not keep going like this. He was afraid of what he might do if the feeling came again at the wrong moment. He was afraid of losing his medical clearance. He was afraid of losing Leilani. But what he said, when I asked him what he hoped for, was this: “I just want to stop looking over my shoulder.”
